newsitem.title: PERU: American nations pledge greater democracy.
newsitem.headline: American nations pledge greater democracy.

text.p: The 34 nations of the Organisation of American States (OAS) opened their 27th annual assembly on Sunday with sweeping pledges to expand democracy and uphold human rights throughout the Western Hemisphere.
OAS Secretary-General Cesar Gaviria said democracy would form the "vertebral column" of the future development of a region notorious in the past for its dictatorial regimes and military uprisings.
Gaviria also urged the world not to stereotype Latin America and the Caribbean based on their problems, but to recognise their efforts to modernise.

"Many identify our hemisphere with the problems that plague it: terrorism, narco-trafficking, corruption, insecurity and poverty," he said in a speech to open the conference. "However, despite these problems, no country is going backwards. Economic reforms, better competition, the growing role of the market continue bringing abundant and welcome changes."

Underscoring its leader's message, the OAS delegates will sign a six-point Lima Declaration affirming democracy and respect for human rights as "the fundamental elements of inter-American cooperation and solidarity."
A preliminary copy of the declaration also promised to step up the war on terrorism, corruption, and trafficking of drugs and arms. But it contained few specifics on how to tackle these issues.
The largely predictable declaration, to be signed at Thursday's close of the assembly, made no reference to the blemished human rights and democracy records of some member nations.
Host country Peru, for example, is under fire for alleged continued abuses in its 17-year war on leftist guerrillas.

The government-controlled Congress unleashed a furore this week when it voted to dismiss three members of Peru's highest constitutional court who were blocking a possible third election bid by President Alberto Fujimori in 2000.
The measure provoked a tide of protest from Peru's opposition, media and public, and also brought rebukes from Washington as a "step backwards" in the nation's democratic process.
Fujimori used the assembly's opening ceremony to defend Peru's democratic credentials and labeled his detractors as being "vested interests" and "corrupt press."

"Here in Peru, just as there is freedom of press, so there is freedom of expression," he said, after his allegation of bribe-taking by journalists brought whistles of protest from the hundreds of reporters covering the event.
Often lambasted as a talking-shop with little real influence, members of the 49-year-old OAS were determined to use the Lima assembly to change its image.
"Let's hope we can make the OAS once again the epicentre of hemispheric dialogue ... the principal instrument of inter- American solidarity and cooperation," Fujimori said.
As well as old problems, the region's new vogues for regional trade accords and free-market reforms were expected to figure high on the OAS' 75-point agenda.
The preliminary Lima Declaration also contained promises to limit resources spent on conventional arms in favour of anti-poverty measures and environmental conservation.
The Peruvian government, still reeling from the four-month Lima hostage crisis, staged a huge security operation to prevent leftist guerrillas from sabotaging the assembly.
Both the Maoist Shining Path and the smaller Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) were planning attacks in Lima around this time, according to anti-terrorist police sources.

The MRTA stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in December, holding 72 VIP hostages for 126 days before troops stormed the building, killed the rebels and freed the captives. One of them died during the rescue operation.

A hero of that hostage crisis, Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, was to chair the assembly's working sessions. One of the most high-ranking of the MRTA's hostages, Tudela narrowly escaped the residence alive after he was shot twice and a grenade exploded at his side in the rescue operation.
Tudela returned to the Foreign Ministry last week. He still uses a wheelchair.
